clusters.name: Your stepfather Desmond and your father Russell in your early teens, 1987–1992
clusters.reason: Around your early secondary school years, several things shifted at once: your distance from Desmond alongside your reaching toward your dad, a separation between your dad and stepmother over having a baby, anxiety climbing as you made the chess squad and then lost your footing with a wrist injury in the first term at the conservatory. When that injury came, you and Rafe had a blow-up and he moved out; you were on your own, getting high and absorbed in fixing radios. By early 1992 you were lost and low, unable to get going, with your grandfather gone the summer before and your mother about to remarry. These shifts pile up in the months around your moving into secondary school and your time at Wexley, with no settlement until you dropped out and moved to the community college.

clusters.name: Your grandfather Gordon's return and your father Russell's marriage to Bettina, 1989–1994
clusters.reason: Around your father's father coming back into the family after years away and your father marrying your stepmother, your own late nights began in earnest and you started playing in the conservatory orchestra. Within months your wrist injury stopped your playing, you and Rafe had a blow-up, and you were on your own getting high, absorbed in radios. By the turn of 1992 you were lost and low. Your grandfather died in June 1991 partway through this; your mother married Desmond that autumn. Your grandmother had thyroid surgery around this time. By early 1994, when you were making a film and stung that your dad had never heard of it, you found your drive again through an exchange in Portugal and raced through the rest of your degree. Your cousin Bella was treated for melanoma around the same time. The shifts settle as you moved forward with your studies.

clusters.name: Your separation from Joelle, 1998–1999
clusters.reason: Around bonding with Joelle in early 1998, your insomnia began getting in the way within a year, yet you were playing the best you ever had and winning competitions. When you separated in the summer of 1999, you started with a therapist. Two of its shifts count—your insomnia and your separation—and the third is your functioning rising as you played at your height; when your separation came, it settled where things shifted and you turned toward help.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Winifred's bowel cancer diagnosis, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Around September 2001, when your grandmother was found to have bowel cancer, you were running out of steam for performing and less content by the month. Within months you had a disastrous audition for the national orchestra in your home town and were done with performing. You were on poor terms with family and friends and left Thornbury for Gull Harbour; you met Marisol that winter and moved with her to Fenwick, then split within the year. Once you were back in Thornbury that winter you sank into a deep depression, hardly moving from the sofa. You could not face your family, yet relied gingerly on friends—Corbin, Dale, and Hamish—and your dad spoke with Corbin during your stay. By January 2004 you began swimming and returned to your therapist; your grandmother died in February. The shifts pile up around her diagnosis and your burnout, with your family distant and your friends close, and things began to settle once you were seeing your therapist again and she had died.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Lorna's death, 2008–2010
clusters.reason: Around your grandmother Lorna's death in January 2008, you were at Alder Creek building with Silas and too drained for conversation with your mother; she pressed to visit, anxiety rising, and you kept the door shut on her. When you left for nursing school in August you cut off from your mother entirely, stopping speaking to her for roughly a year; the silence held until you settled into your programme. Your aunt Imogen had a stroke around this time with months of rehabilitation. Poppy was born in 2010. The shifts fall around your grandmother's death and your move to nursing school, with your mother's push and your response in conflict, then distance opening into cutoff.

clusters.name: Your marriage to Wren, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: Around your marriage to Wren in March 2017, you saw your mother a bit less once she came along. Your cousin Alice was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in her forties in October 2018; your aunt Imogen's memory was slipping and getting worse, and she lashed out when muddled. Your sister Tara married and had a baby on the way; your job steadied and paid well. Yet anxiety rose as you constantly felt you ought to be driving your projects forward, and you started a sleeping pill. By October 2019, Wren was swamped—a street party, then a fundraising dinner, then a drive to the lake for her mother's retirement—and you overfunctioned laying out a plan to settle her. Wren talks with her father and brother all day; nothing happens to one that the others don't hear. Once the weekend had a plan the dinner went well, yet at the lake that night you awoke from the small hours with no more sleep and could only pull back as the others rose; you felt you didn't belong. The shifts cluster around your marriage and Wren's family closeness, with your anxiety and her swamping, and settle as you learned to take shorter, more regular calls with your mother instead.
